/faq/can-arthritis-cause-fatigue.title: Can arthritis cause fatigue? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/can-arthritis-cause-fatigue.description: Yes. Arthritis fatigue is real and common. It's caused by inflammation, chronic pain, poor sleep, and the body fighting disease.
/faq/can-arthritis-cause-fatigue.question: Can arthritis cause fatigue?
/faq/can-arthritis-cause-fatigue.answer: Yes. Arthritis fatigue is real and common. It's caused by inflammation, chronic pain, poor sleep, and the body fighting disease.
/faq/can-arthritis-cause-fatigue.bodyHtml:
What Arthritis Fatigue Feels Like

Arthritis fatigue is a persistent, body-wide exhaustion that rest does not fix. Patients describe it as 'wading through treacle' or waking unrefreshed despite a full night in bed. It often arrives in waves, peaking in the afternoon, and is reported by 40-80% of people with inflammatory arthritis. Unlike normal tiredness it can flatten motivation, concentration and short-term memory, and is frequently rated as more disabling than joint pain itself. Recognising it as a genuine symptom — not laziness — is the first step to managing it well.

Why the Immune System Drives Tiredness

Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-1 cross the blood-brain barrier and trigger 'sickness behaviour' — the same fog you feel during flu. In rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and lupus these chemicals are chronically raised, so the brain receives a constant 'be tired' signal. Anaemia of chronic disease, low iron or low vitamin D often compound the effect. Treating the underlying inflammation with DMARDs or biologics frequently reduces fatigue even when pain scores stay the same.

The Pain-Sleep-Fatigue Loop

Night-time joint pain fragments deep sleep, raising morning inflammatory markers and lowering pain tolerance the next day. This three-way loop is one of the strongest predictors of poor quality of life. Our guide to arthritis and sleep covers practical fixes — supportive pillows, pre-bed analgesia, and a cool dark bedroom. Treat sleep as medicine, not a luxury.

Movement is the Counter-Intuitive Fix

Trial evidence is consistent: graded aerobic exercise reduces fatigue by 20-30% within 8-12 weeks. Begin with 10 minutes of walking, cycling or pool work most days and build slowly. See our best exercises for arthritis for a safe starting plan. Resistance work twice a week also restores the muscle mass that chronic inflammation strips away.

Diet, Hydration and Energy

Anti-inflammatory eating patterns — oily fish, leafy greens, olive oil, nuts and legumes — are linked to lower fatigue scores. Spread protein across meals to support muscle, and keep blood sugar steady with whole grains rather than refined carbohydrates. Mild dehydration alone can drop energy by 10%, so aim for 1.5-2 litres of fluid daily unless your doctor has advised otherwise.

Mental Health Matters

Depression and anxiety roughly double in chronic arthritis and amplify fatigue. Cognitive behavioural therapy, mindfulness and peer support all show measurable benefit. Read more in our arthritis and mental health hub. Speak to your GP if low mood lasts more than two weeks — treatment for the mood often lifts the fatigue too.

When Fatigue Needs Urgent Review

Book a GP appointment if fatigue is worsening rapidly, accompanied by unexplained fever, weight loss, breathlessness or a new rash, or if you cannot complete basic daily tasks. These can signal a flare, anaemia, thyroid dysfunction or medication side-effect that needs prompt investigation.

/faq/arthritis-employment-rights-uk.title: Arthritis at Work: Your Employment Rights (UK)
/faq/arthritis-employment-rights-uk.description: The Equality Act 2010 protects you from discrimination at work and means employers must make reasonable adjustments for arthritis.
/faq/arthritis-employment-rights-uk.question: What are my employment rights with arthritis in the UK?
/faq/arthritis-employment-rights-uk.answer: The Equality Act 2010 protects you from discrimination and requires employers to make 'reasonable adjustments' for your arthritis.
/faq/arthritis-employment-rights-uk.breadcrumb: Arthritis and Employment Rights in the UK
/faq/arthritis-employment-rights-uk.bodyHtml:
Are You Protected by the Equality Act?

Arthritis counts as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 when it has a 'substantial and long-term adverse effect' on day-to-day activities — meaning symptoms expected to last 12 months or more that affect tasks like typing, walking, lifting or concentrating. Protection applies from day one of employment, including during recruitment. You do not need to label yourself 'disabled' to claim these rights; the legal test is functional, not diagnostic. This protection covers direct and indirect discrimination, harassment and victimisation.

Do You Have to Disclose?

There is no legal duty to disclose arthritis to a prospective or current employer, but rights to reasonable adjustments only begin once the employer knows — or could reasonably be expected to know — about your condition. Disclosure can be made to HR or occupational health in confidence, separately from your line manager. Health questions before a job offer are generally unlawful except for specific roles, so any pressure to declare at interview is usually a red flag.

What Counts as a Reasonable Adjustment

Common adjustments include flexible or staggered hours, working from home, ergonomic seating and keyboards, voice-activated software, a parking space close to the entrance, lifts or ground-floor relocation, additional rest breaks, modified duties, and phased returns after a flare. 'Reasonable' is judged on the size of the business, cost, practicality and effect on others. Employers cannot charge you for adjustments and cannot use cost alone as a routine refusal.

Access to Work — A Government Grant

Access to Work is a UK government scheme that funds equipment, travel-to-work costs, support workers and mental-health support that an employer would otherwise have to provide. Self-employed people are eligible too. Apply online at gov.uk; assessments are usually remote and grants can run to several thousand pounds per year. Many people use it for specialist chairs, dictation software or taxi fares during flares.

Occupational Health and Phased Returns

Ask your GP or HR for an occupational health referral. The OH report is independent and carries weight in negotiating adjustments. After a flare or surgery a phased return — reduced hours building back over 4-12 weeks — is standard practice. See our returning to work guide for practical pacing tips.

Flexible Working Requests

From April 2024 all employees can request flexible working from day one, twice in any 12-month period. Submit in writing; the employer must respond within two months and can only refuse on one of eight statutory business grounds. Combining a flexible working request with a reasonable-adjustment request strengthens your position.

Where to Get Help

ACAS offers free confidential advice on 0300 123 1100. Citizens Advice helps with written requests and grievances. Disability Rights UK runs an advice line and produces detailed factsheets. If discrimination is suspected, raise an internal grievance first, then consider an Employment Tribunal claim within three months less one day of the incident.

faqs.q: What are my employment rights with arthritis in the UK?
faqs.a: The Equality Act 2010 protects you from discrimination and requires employers to make 'reasonable adjustments' for your arthritis.

/faq/arthritis-disability-benefits-uk.title: Is Arthritis a Disability in the UK? PIP & Rights
/faq/arthritis-disability-benefits-uk.description: It can be under the Equality Act if it has a long-term effect on daily life. How PIP works for adults, who DLA is for, and your rights at work.
/faq/arthritis-disability-benefits-uk.question: Is arthritis a disability? UK PIP and claim guide
/faq/arthritis-disability-benefits-uk.answer: Arthritis is not automatically a disability. Under the Equality Act 2010 it can be, if a physical impairment has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities. PIP is not awarded from the diagnosis alone. This is educational orientation, not legal advice.
/faq/arthritis-disability-benefits-uk.breadcrumb: Arthritis and Disability Benefits in the UK
/faq/arthritis-disability-benefits-uk.bodyHtml:
Is arthritis a disability under the Equality Act?

Not automatically. GOV.UK says you are disabled under the Equality Act 2010 if you have a physical or mental impairment, and that impairment has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on your ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. Substantial means more than minor or trivial. Long-term means it has lasted, or is likely to last, 12 months or more. Arthritis can meet that test. It depends on the effect, not the diagnosis label. GOV.UK also notes special rules for recurring or fluctuating conditions, such as arthritis, and that the Equality Act 2010 does not apply in Northern Ireland. Read the official definition rather than relying on this page. This is not legal advice.

Is arthritis a disability in the UK?

In England, Scotland and Wales the Equality Act test above is the workplace and services test. It is not a benefits decision. A benefits decision looks at the rules for that benefit. Arthritis is not automatically a disability for either purpose. Say what you cannot do, not only the name of the condition.

Can you get PIP for arthritis?

You might, and you might not. PIP is not based on the diagnosis. It depends on how your condition affects the daily living and mobility activities, using points. Arthritis, including osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis, does not guarantee an award. Check whether daily living or walking is affected. Start a claim on GOV.UK or by phone so the claim date is logged. Keep a diary of what you cannot do safely, repeatedly, to an acceptable standard, and in a reasonable time. A decision is about points, not the label. See GOV.UK PIP and this site’s PIP guide. This is not a prediction of the result.

What does a PIP claim look at?

Daily living activities, such as cooking, washing, dressing, and managing treatment, and mobility, including planning a journey and moving around. You count as able to do an activity only if you can do it reliably: safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly, and in a reasonable time. The later sections on this page describe those activities in more detail. They are not a promise of points.

Can I claim disability allowance for osteoarthritis in the UK?

There is no separate osteoarthritis allowance. For new claims by adults in England and Wales, the usual route is PIP, not Disability Living Allowance. DLA is mainly for children under 16, or for adults who already have a DLA award. Osteoarthritis does not qualify you by name. PIP still depends on daily living and mobility. People over State Pension age who are not already on PIP usually look at Attendance Allowance instead, which has no mobility part. Confirm the current route on GOV.UK.

PIP for osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis uses the same PIP activities as any other condition. Knee, hip, or spine pain often comes up under moving around, and hand osteoarthritis often comes up under cooking, washing, or dressing. Distance on one good walk is not the whole story if you cannot repeat it safely. There is no osteoarthritis rate and no success rate on this page.

Workplace rights are reasonable adjustments, not a guarantee

If arthritis meets the Equality Act test, an employer may have to consider reasonable adjustments, such as hours, equipment, or duties. The diagnosis alone does not force a particular change, and this page cannot say what is reasonable in your job. Workplace detail sits on our employment-rights FAQ. This is not legal advice.

Access to Work

Access to Work is a GOV.UK scheme that can help with work costs, such as equipment or travel, if a health condition affects your job. It is not PIP and it is not guaranteed. Apply through the official Access to Work page on GOV.UK. One short note is enough here; check the live rules there.

Personal Independence Payment (PIP): who can claim

PIP is for people aged 16 up to State Pension age. It is not means-tested, is not affected by savings, and you can claim it whether you work or not. It is paid because of how arthritis affects you day to day, not because of your diagnosis or your scan results. To qualify you normally need to have had the difficulties for at least three months and expect them to continue for at least a further nine months. In Scotland, PIP has been replaced by Adult Disability Payment, which uses the same points-based tests but is administered by Social Security Scotland.

How PIP is scored for arthritis symptoms

PIP has two parts: daily living and mobility. An assessor scores you against ten daily living activities (preparing food, eating, managing medication and therapy, washing and bathing, managing toilet needs, dressing and undressing, communicating, reading, mixing with others, and managing money) and two mobility activities (planning and following a journey, and moving around). Eight points in a part gives the standard rate; twelve points gives the enhanced rate. Hand and wrist arthritis commonly scores under preparing food, dressing and washing — for example, needing an aid such as a jar opener, a perching stool, a long-handled sponge, a shower seat, or a button hook. Knee, hip, foot and spinal arthritis usually score under moving around, which is graded by how far you can walk: less than 20 metres, 20 to 50 metres, 50 to 200 metres, or more than 200 metres.

PIP eligibility with hand, wrist and finger arthritis

Hand arthritis is assessed by task, not by grip strength or X-ray changes. The daily living activities it most often affects are preparing food (chopping and peeling), taking nutrition (holding cutlery or a full mug), managing medication (blister packs and bottle tops), washing and bathing (getting in and out, holding a sponge), managing toilet needs, dressing (buttons, zips, bra fastenings, laces) and communicating or reading if you cannot hold a phone, pen or book. Needing an aid — jar opener, kettle tipper, button hook, long-handled sponge, electric toothbrush, adapted cutlery — usually scores two points for that activity, and several two-point scores add up to the eight needed for the standard rate. Needing another person to help, rather than an aid, scores higher. Say clearly if you can manage on a good day but not during a flare, and if hand pain means a task takes far longer or has to be broken into stages.

Osteoarthritis and the PIP mobility score

The moving around activity is scored purely on distance walked reliably — safely, repeatedly, in a reasonable time. Standing and then moving more than 200 metres scores zero; more than 50 but no more than 200 metres scores four points; more than 20 but no more than 50 metres scores eight points (standard rate); more than 1 but no more than 20 metres scores twelve points (enhanced rate); and being unable to stand or move more than one metre, even with an aid, scores twelve. Knee, hip, foot and spinal osteoarthritis often means a person can reach 200 metres once, then cannot repeat it that day or needs to stop and rest — that is not walking the distance reliably, so describe the pain level, the stops, the recovery time and what happens on the way back. Using a stick, crutch or scaffolding along the route is relevant and should be stated. The second mobility activity, planning and following a journey, covers anxiety, disorientation or needing someone with you, and is scored separately.

The "reliably" rule most arthritis claims turn on

You only count as able to do an activity if you can do it reliably — safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly as often as you reasonably need to, and in a reasonable time (broadly no more than twice as long as someone without your condition). This matters enormously in arthritis, where the honest answer is often "yes, but". If you can climb into the bath but risk falling, if you can chop vegetables but not twice in a day, if you can walk 100 metres but only once and then need to rest for an hour, or if morning stiffness means dressing takes 45 minutes, say so in exactly those terms. Describe a bad day and a flare as well as a good day, and give the rough proportion of days each applies — the rules say an activity counts if it applies on more than half the days over a year.

Evidence that strengthens an arthritis claim

Send what you already have rather than waiting for new letters: rheumatology or orthopaedic clinic letters, X-ray or MRI reports, your repeat prescription list (DMARDs, biologics, steroid injections, opioids), physiotherapy or occupational therapy notes, an OT home assessment, and any Blue Badge or aids and adaptations record. A short diary covering two weeks — how long you took to dress, how far you walked, how many days you could not cook — is often more persuasive than a GP letter, because it maps directly onto the descriptors. Keep a copy of everything you send.

Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) and Universal Credit

If arthritis limits your ability to work, new-style ESA is based on your National Insurance record; otherwise the limited capability for work element of Universal Credit does the same job. Both use the Work Capability Assessment, which is a separate test from PIP with its own descriptors — you can be found fit for work and still receive PIP, and vice versa. You will need a fit note from your GP while your assessment is pending.

Other benefits and passported help

Attendance Allowance is for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care and has no mobility component. Disability Living Allowance is mainly for children under 16, or for adults who already have a DLA award. New adult claims in England and Wales are PIP, not DLA. Carer's Allowance may be claimable by someone who cares for you for 35 hours or more a week, if you get a qualifying rate of PIP daily living. A PIP award can also passport you to a Blue Badge, a disabled person's railcard or bus pass, Motability (enhanced mobility rate), council tax reductions and reduced water charges. Check these separately — they are not awarded automatically.

How to apply, step by step

Start the claim by phoning the DWP PIP new claims line or applying online; the claim date is set when you first make contact, so start it before you gather paperwork. You will then be sent the PIP2 form, "How your disability affects you", which you normally have one month to return — ring and ask for extra time if you need it. Use the extra information box, and answer each activity in the language of the reliably rule. Most assessments are now by telephone or video, though face-to-face still happens. Free help with forms is available from Citizens Advice, your local welfare rights service, and hospital rheumatology social workers.

If you are refused: mandatory reconsideration and appeal

If you are refused, you can ask for the decision to be looked at again. This page does not quote a success rate. You have one month from the decision letter to ask for a mandatory reconsideration, and it is worth requesting the assessor's report first so you can answer it point by point. If the reconsideration fails, you have one month to appeal to an independent tribunal using form SSCS1. You can attend the hearing in person or by video. Citizens Advice or a welfare rights adviser can represent you free of charge. This page does not quote appeal success rates.

Where to check current rates

PIP, ESA and Attendance Allowance rates change each April, so check the current figures on GOV.UK rather than relying on any figure quoted in an article. If you are unsure which benefits apply to your household, a free benefits calculator from Turn2us or entitledto will model your situation in a few minutes. If money worries are affecting your health or mood, talk to your GP as well — financial stress and pain feed each other.

/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.title: What are the best exercises for people with arthritis? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.description: Low-impact exercises like walking, swimming, and gentle strength training are ideal. They reduce pain, improve mobility, and strengthen muscles around joints.
/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.question: What are the best exercises for people with arthritis?
/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.answer: Low-impact exercises like walking, swimming, and gentle strength training are ideal. They reduce pain, improve mobility, and strengthen muscles around joints.
/faq/best-exercises-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Low-Impact Cardio

Walking (30 mins, 5 days/week), swimming, water aerobics, cycling, elliptical trainer. These get your heart rate up without stressing joints.

Strength Training

Strong muscles support joints. Use light weights, resistance bands, or bodyweight (push-ups against wall, squats). Do 2-3 times/week. Start light and progress gradually.

Flexibility & Stretching

Yoga (gentle classes), tai chi, daily stretching. Hold stretches 15-30 seconds. This reduces stiffness and improves range of motion.

Tips for Safe Exercise

Warm up 5 mins first, stop if sharp pain develops (mild discomfort OK), ice after if swollen, rest days between workouts, work with a physiotherapist initially.

/faq/reduce-arthritis-pain-naturally.title: How can I reduce arthritis pain naturally? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/reduce-arthritis-pain-naturally.description: Heat therapy, gentle exercise, anti-inflammatory foods, weight management, sleep, and stress reduction all reduce arthritis pain without medication.
/faq/reduce-arthritis-pain-naturally.question: How can I reduce arthritis pain naturally?
/faq/reduce-arthritis-pain-naturally.answer: Heat therapy, gentle exercise, anti-inflammatory foods, weight management, sleep, and stress reduction all reduce arthritis pain without medication.
/faq/reduce-arthritis-pain-naturally.breadcrumb: How to Reduce Arthritis Pain Naturally
/faq/reduce-arthritis-pain-naturally.bodyHtml:
Heat & Cold Therapy

Heat (hot water bottle, warm bath, heating pad) reduces stiffness. Cold (ice pack) reduces swelling. Use 15-20 mins at a time. Test which helps you most.

Anti-Inflammatory Foods

Omega-3 fish, olive oil, colourful vegetables, berries, nuts, turmeric, ginger. These contain natural compounds that reduce inflammation.

Gentle Movement

Walking, swimming, yoga, tai chi. Movement reduces pain more than rest in most cases. Start gently.

Sleep, Stress, Weight

Good sleep helps inflammation. Stress worsens pain (try meditation). Extra weight stresses joints (even 5kg loss helps).

faqs.q: How can I reduce arthritis pain naturally?
faqs.a: Heat therapy, gentle exercise, anti-inflammatory foods, weight management, sleep, and stress reduction all reduce arthritis pain without medication.

/faq/what-is-osteoarthritis.title: What is osteoarthritis? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/what-is-osteoarthritis.description: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis, caused by wear and tear of cartilage. It typically affects the knees, hips, hands, and spine.
/faq/what-is-osteoarthritis.question: What is osteoarthritis?
/faq/what-is-osteoarthritis.answer: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis, caused by wear and tear of cartilage. It typically affects the knees, hips, hands, and spine.
/faq/what-is-osteoarthritis.bodyHtml:
How Osteoarthritis Develops

Cartilage (smooth tissue covering bones) gradually wears away, causing pain, stiffness, and inflammation. It usually develops slowly over years. Risk factors: age, female sex, previous injury, obesity, family history.

Symptoms

Joint pain (especially with activity), stiffness (especially morning), swelling, reduced movement, creaking sounds, pain in bad weather.

Treatment

Pain relief, anti-inflammatory drugs, injections, exercise, weight management, heat therapy. Surgery for severe cases.

Can It Be Prevented?

No guaranteed prevention, but manage weight, stay active, protect joints from injury, eat well, and manage related conditions.

faqs.q: What is osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis, caused by wear and tear of cartilage. It typically affects the knees, hips, hands, and spine.

/faq/what-is-rheumatoid-arthritis.title: What is rheumatoid arthritis? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/what-is-rheumatoid-arthritis.description: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks joints, causing swelling, pain, and fatigue.
/faq/what-is-rheumatoid-arthritis.question: What is rheumatoid arthritis?
/faq/what-is-rheumatoid-arthritis.answer: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks joints, causing swelling, pain, and fatigue.
/faq/what-is-rheumatoid-arthritis.bodyHtml:
What Happens in RA

Your immune system mistakenly attacks the joints' protective lining, causing inflammation, swelling, pain, and eventually joint damage. Affects hands, feet, and other joints. More serious than OA.

Symptoms

Joint pain and swelling (usually hands, feet, wrists), morning stiffness (over 30 mins), fatigue, low-grade fever, depression.

Diagnosis & Treatment

Blood tests (rheumatoid factor, CCP), ultrasound, X-rays. Treatment: DMARDs (disease-modifying drugs), biologics, pain relief, physiotherapy, lifestyle changes.

Living Well with RA

Early aggressive treatment is key. Most people can achieve remission or low disease activity with modern drugs. Work closely with your rheumatologist.

faqs.q: What is rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks joints, causing swelling, pain, and fatigue.

/faq/what-is-juvenile-arthritis.title: What is juvenile arthritis? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/what-is-juvenile-arthritis.description: Juvenile arthritis is arthritis in children under 16. Despite the name, it can persist into adulthood and requires early, aggressive treatment.
/faq/what-is-juvenile-arthritis.question: What is juvenile arthritis?
/faq/what-is-juvenile-arthritis.answer: Juvenile arthritis is arthritis in children under 16. Despite the name, it can persist into adulthood and requires early, aggressive treatment.
/faq/what-is-juvenile-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Types of Juvenile Arthritis

Oligoarticular JA (1-4 joints affected), polyarticular JA (5+ joints), systemic JA (fever, rash, whole-body symptoms). Each requires different treatment.

Impact on Children

Can affect growth, school attendance, social development, self-esteem. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent permanent joint damage.

Treatment

DMARDs, biologics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychology support. Prognosis has improved dramatically with modern medications.

Support Available

Specialist paediatric rheumatologists, school support, summer camps for kids with JA, benefits/allowances, family counselling.

faqs.q: What is juvenile arthritis?
faqs.a: Juvenile arthritis is arthritis in children under 16. Despite the name, it can persist into adulthood and requires early, aggressive treatment.

/faq/can-arthritis-affect-young-people.title: Can arthritis affect younger people? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/can-arthritis-affect-young-people.description: Yes. Arthritis isn't just for older people. Rheumatoid arthritis often develops in people 40-60, but any type can develop at any age, including teenagers.
/faq/can-arthritis-affect-young-people.question: Can arthritis affect younger people?
/faq/can-arthritis-affect-young-people.answer: Yes. Arthritis isn't just for older people. Rheumatoid arthritis often develops in people 40-60, but any type can develop at any age, including teenagers.
/faq/can-arthritis-affect-young-people.bodyHtml:
Arthritis in Young Adults

Rheumatoid arthritis commonly develops in 30-50 year olds (more women). Osteoarthritis can develop in people 30+ with previous injuries. Living with arthritis as a young person brings unique challenges: work, relationships, appearance concerns.

Arthritis in Children

Juvenile arthritis affects about 12,000 UK children. It's an autoimmune condition. Early treatment prevents permanent damage.

Impact on Young People

Young people often feel isolated, struggle with peer relationships, worry about future, face barriers at work, manage medication side effects. Psychological support is important.

Support & Resources

Young people's arthritis services, online support groups, workplace support, school assistance, benefits if eligible.

faqs.a: Yes. Arthritis isn't just for older people. Rheumatoid arthritis often develops in people 40-60, but any type can develop at any age, including teenagers.

/faq/is-arthritis-a-disability.title: Is arthritis considered a disability? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/is-arthritis-a-disability.description: Legally, yes — if it substantially limits your ability to do normal activities. This means you're protected by the Equality Act 2010.
/faq/is-arthritis-a-disability.question: Is arthritis considered a disability?
/faq/is-arthritis-a-disability.answer: Legally, yes — if it substantially limits your ability to do normal activities. This means you're protected by the Equality Act 2010.
/faq/is-arthritis-a-disability.bodyHtml:
Legal Definition

Under UK law, arthritis is a disability if it substantially and long-term limits your ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities. This includes work, self-care, mobility, relationships.

What 'Substantial' Means

More than minor or trivial impact. If arthritis stops you doing something most people do, it's substantial. Examples: unable to walk far, can't dress yourself, can't work full-time.

Your Rights

Protection from discrimination, access to reasonable adjustments, eligibility for benefits, right to flexible working, occupational health support at work.

Telling People

You don't have to disclose disability to employers unless you need adjustments. Some people worry about stigma, but disclosure often helps.

faqs.q: Is arthritis considered a disability?
faqs.a: Legally, yes — if it substantially limits your ability to do normal activities. This means you're protected by the Equality Act 2010.

/faq/arthritis-and-pregnancy.title: How does arthritis affect pregnancy? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/arthritis-and-pregnancy.description: Many women find arthritis improves during pregnancy due to immune changes. However, some find it worsens. Plan ahead with your rheumatologist.
/faq/arthritis-and-pregnancy.question: How does arthritis affect pregnancy?
/faq/arthritis-and-pregnancy.answer: Many women find arthritis improves during pregnancy due to immune changes. However, some find it worsens. Plan ahead with your rheumatologist.
/faq/arthritis-and-pregnancy.bodyHtml:
Can You Have Children With Arthritis?

Yes. Most women with arthritis have safe, healthy pregnancies and healthy babies. The condition itself rarely affects fertility, although some medications can. The key is planning ahead with a rheumatologist who specialises in pregnancy — ideally three to six months before trying to conceive — so disease activity is low and any teratogenic medication has been safely switched. Men with arthritis should also have a preconception review because some drugs (notably methotrexate and leflunomide) need stopping before conception.

How Pregnancy Changes Arthritis

Around 60-70% of women with rheumatoid arthritis improve during pregnancy, often dramatically in the second and third trimesters, due to immune-modulating effects of pregnancy hormones. Lupus and axial spondyloarthritis can be less predictable and may flare. Osteoarthritis tends to stay the same or worsen mechanically as weight increases and ligaments soften. Hand and knee pain in late pregnancy are common and usually settle within months of delivery.

Medication Safety in Pregnancy

Hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, azathioprine, ciclosporin and most TNF-inhibitor biologics (especially certolizumab) have substantial safety data and can usually continue. Methotrexate, leflunomide, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide and JAK inhibitors must be stopped before conception. NSAIDs are best avoided after 20 weeks. Low-dose prednisolone, paracetamol and short courses of opioids are generally considered safe. Never stop a DMARD without specialist advice — uncontrolled disease is itself a pregnancy risk.

Labour, Delivery and Pain Relief

Most women can plan a vaginal delivery. Hip, knee or spine involvement may need extra positioning support — discuss this in advance with your midwife. Epidural anaesthesia is usually possible but a senior anaesthetic review is wise if the cervical spine, jaw or hips are affected. A short antenatal physiotherapy appointment to practise labour positions is invaluable.

The Postpartum Flare

Rheumatoid arthritis flares within three to six months of delivery in roughly half of women, partly driven by falling pregnancy hormones and broken sleep. Restart maintenance DMARDs promptly — most are compatible with breastfeeding, including hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and TNF inhibitors. Arrange extra help with lifting and night feeds, and book a rheumatology review within the first six weeks.

Breastfeeding With Arthritis

Breastfeeding is possible for almost all women with arthritis. Side-lying positions and supportive cushions protect sore wrists, elbows and shoulders. Most modern DMARDs and biologics transfer in minimal amounts and are considered compatible. Methotrexate, leflunomide and cyclophosphamide remain contraindicated. The Breastfeeding Network Drugs in Breastmilk service offers free written advice.

Emotional Support and Looking Ahead

Postnatal depression is twice as common in mothers with chronic illness. Build a support network early, accept help with childcare, and read our arthritis and mental health guide. With planning, most parents with arthritis raise children safely and confidently — the disease shapes the journey, it does not prevent it.

faqs.q: How does arthritis affect pregnancy?
faqs.a: Many women find arthritis improves during pregnancy due to immune changes. However, some find it worsens. Plan ahead with your rheumatologist.

/faq/arthritis-and-sleep.title: Why does arthritis cause sleep problems? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/arthritis-and-sleep.description: Pain and inflammation keep you awake and reduce sleep quality. Poor sleep worsens arthritis. Breaking this cycle is important.
/faq/arthritis-and-sleep.question: Why does arthritis cause sleep problems?
/faq/arthritis-and-sleep.answer: Pain and inflammation keep you awake and reduce sleep quality. Poor sleep worsens arthritis. Breaking this cycle is important.
/faq/arthritis-and-sleep.bodyHtml:
Why Arthritis Disrupts Sleep

Joint pain wakes you at night, morning stiffness worse with poor sleep, inflammation rises at night, anxiety/depression reduce sleep quality, some medications disrupt sleep.

The Sleep-Arthritis Cycle

Poor sleep worsens inflammation, which worsens pain, which worsens sleep. Breaking this cycle is crucial.

Sleep Tips for Arthritis

Take pain relief before bed, use pillows for joint support, keep bedroom cool and dark, try relaxation (meditation, breathing), avoid caffeine after 2pm, establish routine, exercise during day (not evening).

When to Seek Help

If sleep problems persist, ask GP about sleep aids (short-term), cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), review medications, check for sleep apnoea.

faqs.q: Why does arthritis cause sleep problems?
faqs.a: Pain and inflammation keep you awake and reduce sleep quality. Poor sleep worsens arthritis. Breaking this cycle is important.

/faq/arthritis-flare-management.title: What should I do when I have an arthritis flare? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/arthritis-flare-management.description: Rest affected joints, use ice, take pain relief, maintain some gentle movement, rest more than usual, and contact your doctor if it worsens.
/faq/arthritis-flare-management.question: What should I do when I have an arthritis flare?
/faq/arthritis-flare-management.answer: Rest affected joints, use ice, take pain relief, maintain some gentle movement, rest more than usual, and contact your doctor if it worsens.
/faq/arthritis-flare-management.breadcrumb: What to Do During an Arthritis Flare
/faq/arthritis-flare-management.bodyHtml:
Recognising a Flare Early

A flare is a sudden worsening of joint pain, swelling, stiffness and fatigue that lasts more than 24 hours and is clearly out of pattern for you. Early warning signs include heavier morning stiffness, low-grade fever, sleep disturbance, brain fog and a 'flu-ish' malaise the day before joints swell. Keeping a simple symptom diary — sleep, steps, mood, stress, food, weather — helps you spot triggers and intervene 24-48 hours earlier each time, which shortens flare duration significantly.

Common Triggers to Audit

The most reported triggers are viral infections, emotional stress, missed or late medication, sudden weather changes, sleep loss, alcohol binges, ultra-processed food, dehydration and overdoing activity on a good day. Hormonal shifts and travel are also frequent. You cannot avoid every trigger, but identifying your top two or three lets you build prevention into normal life rather than reacting after the flare has started.

The First 48 Hours: Rest, Ice, Elevate

Reduce load on the affected joints — sit when possible, swap a long walk for pool work or none at all. Apply a wrapped ice pack for 15-20 minutes every 2-3 hours for the first day to settle acute swelling, then switch to heat for morning stiffness. Take regular pain relief as prescribed rather than waiting for pain to peak. Aim for 8-9 hours of sleep and prioritise hydration.

48-72 Hour Protocol

Begin gentle range-of-motion movement every couple of hours — even five slow circles or stretches stops joints stiffening. Eat anti-inflammatory meals (oily fish, leafy greens, berries, olive oil) and avoid alcohol. Use splints only briefly to rest very painful hands or wrists; prolonged immobilisation weakens muscle and worsens recovery. Cancel non-essential commitments without guilt — recovery is the priority.

When to Contact Your GP or Rheumatology Team

Call within 24 hours if you develop a fever above 38°C, a new hot swollen joint that could indicate infection, chest pain, breathlessness, a new rash, or if symptoms are not improving after 72 hours of self-care. Septic arthritis is an emergency. If you are on biologics or DMARDs, your rheumatology helpline can often adjust medication or arrange a steroid injection or short oral steroid course.

Activity Pacing and the Return to Normal

Reintroduce activity at 50% of your pre-flare baseline and add roughly 10% per day. Use the 'two-day rule' — if pain is worse two days after an activity, the dose was too high. Our best exercises for arthritis guide includes gentle resumption plans for knees, hips and hands.

Preventing the Next Flare

After every flare, review what came before it and pick one change for next time — earlier medication, better sleep, more hydration, or saying no to one extra commitment. Long-term, consistent low-impact exercise, anti-inflammatory eating, stress management and never skipping DMARDs cut flare frequency by 30-50% in most studies.

faqs.q: What should I do when I have an arthritis flare?
faqs.a: Rest affected joints, use ice, take pain relief, maintain some gentle movement, rest more than usual, and contact your doctor if it worsens.

/faq/returning-to-work-arthritis.title: How do I return to work after arthritis diagnosis? | Living With Arthritis
/faq/returning-to-work-arthritis.description: Work with occupational health, request reasonable adjustments, plan gradual return, communicate with your manager, and take breaks as needed.
/faq/returning-to-work-arthritis.question: How do I return to work after arthritis diagnosis?
/faq/returning-to-work-arthritis.answer: Work with occupational health, request reasonable adjustments, plan gradual return, communicate with your manager, and take breaks as needed.
/faq/returning-to-work-arthritis.bodyHtml:
Preparing to Return

Talk to occupational health, plan adjustments needed (equipment, hours, tasks), inform manager/HR (if you choose), get medical support letter, plan gradual return if needed.

Reasonable Adjustments

Flexible hours, remote working, ergonomic equipment (chair, desk, keyboard), frequent breaks, modified duties, accessible facilities, understanding manager.

Managing Work

Pacing (don't overdo first week back), communicate if struggling, use lunch breaks to rest, don't hide pain (management helps), attend occupational health reviews.

Long-Term Work Success

Build good relationships, maintain open communication, review adjustments regularly, manage stress and workload, think long-term not short-term, consider career development alongside arthritis.

faqs.q: How do I return to work after arthritis diagnosis?
faqs.a: Work with occupational health, request reasonable adjustments, plan gradual return, communicate with your manager, and take breaks as needed.
